questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Urinary stones, BPH, hematuria
questions.stem: Which imaging is the investigation of choice for acute renal colic?
options: Non-contrast computed tomography of the kidneys, ureters and bladder
questions.concept: It detects stones of almost any composition including radiolucent uric acid stones, defines size and site, and identifies alternative diagnoses, though ultrasound is preferred in pregnancy and in children.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Urinary Tract

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Urinary stones, BPH, hematuria
questions.stem: Which stone type is radiolucent on plain radiography and may dissolve with urinary alkalinisation?
questions.concept: Alkalinising the urine to a pH above 6.5 with potassium citrate, with allopurinol where indicated, can dissolve these stones, which is the only stone type reliably amenable to medical dissolution.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Urinary Tract

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Urinary stones, BPH, hematuria
questions.stem: Which organism is associated with struvite staghorn calculi, and by what mechanism?
options: Urease-producing organisms such as Proteus, which raise urinary pH and precipitate magnesium ammonium phosphate
questions.concept: Because the stone harbours bacteria, complete surgical clearance rather than antibiotics alone is required, and residual fragments cause recurrent infection.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Urinary Tract

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Urinary stones, BPH, hematuria
questions.stem: Which stone size and location is most likely to pass spontaneously with medical expulsive therapy?
options: A stone under 5 mm in the distal ureter
A 10 mm stone in the proximal ureter
questions.concept: Analgesia with hydration and, in selected cases, an alpha blocker supports passage, while larger or proximal stones and any obstruction with infection require intervention.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Urinary Tract

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Urinary stones, BPH, hematuria
questions.stem: Which presentation of urolithiasis requires emergency decompression rather than elective treatment?
options: An obstructed infected system with fever and systemic sepsis
A 4 mm stone with microscopic haematuria
questions.concept: Percutaneous nephrostomy or a ureteric stent relieves the obstruction, and definitive stone treatment is deferred until the infection is controlled because instrumenting an infected system can precipitate septic shock.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Urinary Tract

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Urinary stones, BPH, hematuria
questions.stem: Which class of drug shrinks the prostate over months by inhibiting conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone?
options: A 5-alpha reductase inhibitor such as finasteride
An alpha blocker such as tamsulosin
questions.concept: Alpha blockers relieve symptoms within days by relaxing smooth muscle, whereas 5-alpha reductase inhibitors take 6 months, reduce prostate volume and lower the risk of retention and surgery, and they halve the prostate-specific antigen.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Urinary Tract

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Urinary stones, BPH, hematuria
questions.stem: Why does painless visible haematuria in an adult require full urinary tract investigation even if it settles?
options: It is the cardinal presentation of urothelial malignancy, and intermittency does not reduce the risk
It is always due to infection
questions.concept: Evaluation combines upper tract imaging with cystoscopy, because ultrasound alone misses small bladder tumours and cytology has limited sensitivity for low-grade disease.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Urinary Tract

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Urology: renal, bladder & testicular tumours; hydrocele, phimosis
questions.stem: Which finding on transillumination and palpation distinguishes a hydrocele from a testicular tumour?
options: A hydrocele transilluminates and the testis cannot be felt separately, whereas a tumour is opaque and hard
questions.concept: Ultrasound is used when the testis cannot be palpated, because a tumour with a secondary hydrocele must not be mistaken for a simple one.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Kidneys and Genitourinary Tract

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Urology: renal, bladder & testicular tumours; hydrocele, phimosis
questions.stem: Which tumour marker pattern indicates a non-seminomatous element in a testicular germ cell tumour?
options: A raised placental alkaline phosphatase only
questions.concept: Pure seminoma never raises alpha-fetoprotein, so its elevation mandates treatment as a non-seminomatous tumour regardless of the histology reported.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Kidneys and Genitourinary Tract

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Urology: renal, bladder & testicular tumours; hydrocele, phimosis
questions.stem: Which surgical approach is used for a suspected testicular tumour, and why?
options: Inguinal orchidectomy with high cord ligation, avoiding a scrotal incision which would alter lymphatic drainage
questions.concept: Testicular lymphatics drain to the para-aortic nodes along the cord, so violating the scrotum introduces inguinal nodal spread and complicates staging and radiotherapy planning.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Kidneys and Genitourinary Tract

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Urology: renal, bladder & testicular tumours; hydrocele, phimosis
questions.stem: Which type of bladder cancer is associated with chronic schistosomiasis, and how does it differ in behaviour?
options: Squamous cell carcinoma, which tends to be muscle-invasive at presentation and less responsive to intravesical therapy
questions.concept: In non-endemic areas urothelial carcinoma predominates and smoking is the main risk factor, and most cases present as non-muscle-invasive disease managed by resection with intravesical therapy.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Kidneys and Genitourinary Tract

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Urology: renal, bladder & testicular tumours; hydrocele, phimosis
questions.stem: Which intravesical agent reduces recurrence and progression in high-risk non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer?
options: Mitomycin as the preferred agent for high risk
questions.concept: Mitomycin is used for intermediate-risk disease and as a single postoperative instillation, whereas BCG with maintenance is standard for high-grade and carcinoma in situ.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Kidneys and Genitourinary Tract

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Urology: renal, bladder & testicular tumours; hydrocele, phimosis
questions.stem: Why is circumcision indicated for pathological phimosis but not for physiological non-retractility in a young boy?
options: Balanitis xerotica obliterans produces a scarred non-retractile prepuce that will not resolve, whereas physiological adhesions separate spontaneously with growth
questions.concept: Forcible retraction of a physiologically adherent foreskin causes scarring and can create the very problem the operation would then be needed to correct.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Kidneys and Genitourinary Tract

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Vascular surgery, varicose veins & peripheral arterial disease
questions.stem: Which bedside measurement quantifies the severity of peripheral arterial disease, and what value indicates critical ischaemia?
options: The ankle brachial pressure index, with a value below 0.4 indicating critical ischaemia
Capillary refill time, with 3 seconds indicating critical ischaemia
questions.concept: The index is falsely high in diabetes and renal failure because of medial calcification, in which case toe pressures or transcutaneous oxygen measurement are used instead.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. Arterial and Venous Disorders

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Vascular surgery, varicose veins & peripheral arterial disease
questions.stem: Which intervention gives the greatest improvement in walking distance in stable intermittent claudication?
options: A supervised exercise programme with smoking cessation and best medical therapy
questions.concept: Because claudication rarely progresses to limb loss, the priorities are cardiovascular risk reduction with a statin and antiplatelet and functional improvement, with intervention reserved for lifestyle-limiting or critical disease.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. Arterial and Venous Disorders

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Vascular surgery, varicose veins & peripheral arterial disease
questions.stem: Which classification describes the six-hour window and the features distinguishing viable from irreversibly ischaemic limb?
options: The Rutherford classification of acute limb ischaemia, based on sensory loss, motor deficit and Doppler signals
questions.concept: A limb with profound paralysis and absent Doppler signals is irreversible and requires amputation, whereas a threatened limb requires immediate revascularisation.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. Arterial and Venous Disorders

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Vascular surgery, varicose veins & peripheral arterial disease
questions.stem: Which finding indicates that a varicose vein problem arises from saphenofemoral incompetence?
options: Reflux at the saphenofemoral junction on duplex ultrasound with a positive tourniquet test at the groin
questions.concept: Duplex has replaced clinical tests as the mapping tool, and treatment is directed at the highest point of reflux, most often by endovenous thermal or chemical ablation.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. Arterial and Venous Disorders

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Vascular surgery, varicose veins & peripheral arterial disease
questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes a venous from an arterial leg ulcer?
options: A shallow ulcer in the gaiter area with surrounding pigmentation and oedema, with palpable pulses
A deep punched-out ulcer over the malleolus with absent pulses
A painless plantar ulcer with intact pulses
An ulcer with rolled everted edges
questions.concept: Compression is the treatment for venous ulceration but is dangerous in arterial disease, which is why the ankle brachial index must be measured before bandaging.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. Arterial and Venous Disorders

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Vascular surgery, varicose veins & peripheral arterial disease
questions.stem: Why is an abdominal aortic aneurysm repaired at a diameter of about 5.5 cm rather than earlier?
options: Below that size the annual rupture risk is lower than the operative mortality, so surveillance is safer
Repair is technically impossible when smaller
The diameter cannot be measured accurately
questions.concept: Rapid expansion of more than 1 cm per year, symptoms, or a lower threshold in women shift the balance toward earlier repair, and the decision is individualised.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. Arterial and Venous Disorders

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Wound healing, surgical site infection & sutures
questions.stem: Which phase of wound healing accounts for the gain in tensile strength over weeks to months?
options: The maturation and remodelling phase, with replacement of type III by cross-linked type I collagen
questions.concept: Tensile strength is only about 10 percent at one week and plateaus at 70 to 80 percent of normal, so a wound never regains its original strength.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. Wound Healing and Surgical Infection

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Wound healing, surgical site infection & sutures
questions.stem: Which classification of surgical wound carries the highest expected infection rate?
options: Dirty or infected, as in surgery on established infection or perforated viscus
questions.concept: Expected rates rise from under 2 percent for clean wounds to over 25 percent for dirty wounds, which is why the classification guides prophylaxis and consent.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. Wound Healing and Surgical Infection

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Wound healing, surgical site infection & sutures
questions.stem: Which suture material is absorbable, monofilament and suitable for a subcuticular closure?
questions.concept: Monofilament materials harbour fewer bacteria than braided ones, and matching the absorption time to the tissue healing rate governs the choice, with polydioxanone lasting far longer than poliglecaprone.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. Wound Healing and Surgical Infection

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Wound healing, surgical site infection & sutures
questions.stem: Which factor most strongly increases the risk of surgical site infection and is modifiable before elective surgery?
options: Smoking, along with poor glycaemic control, obesity and malnutrition
questions.concept: Perioperative normothermia, normoglycaemia, appropriate hair removal with clippers and correctly timed antibiotic prophylaxis form the evidence-based bundle for prevention.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. Wound Healing and Surgical Infection

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Wound healing, surgical site infection & sutures
questions.stem: Which timing of antibiotic prophylaxis achieves the lowest surgical site infection rate?
options: Within 60 minutes before skin incision, with redosing for long operations or major blood loss
At induction of anaesthesia only for clean cases
questions.concept: Prolonging prophylaxis beyond 24 hours adds resistance and Clostridioides difficile risk without reducing infection, which is a central stewardship message in surgery.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. Wound Healing and Surgical Infection

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Wound healing, surgical site infection & sutures
questions.stem: Why does a wound heal by secondary intention with more contraction and a worse scar than one closed primarily?
options: The larger tissue defect is filled by granulation tissue with abundant myofibroblasts, which contract the wound margins
questions.concept: This is why contractures form across joints and why grafting or flap cover is used to prevent functional loss in large defects.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. Wound Healing and Surgical Infection
